item.title: $35m sawmill to lift forestry
item.description: PRIME Minister Sitiveni Rabuka has hailed the $35million Tropik Wood Industries carriage sawmill project in Drasa, Lautoka as a major step in transforming Fiji’s forestry sector and unlocking greater value from mahogany resources. item.content:encoded:
PRIME Minister Sitiveni Rabuka has hailed the $35million Tropik Wood Industries carriage sawmill project in Drasa, Lautoka as a major step in transforming Fiji’s forestry sector and unlocking greater value from mahogany resources.

Mr Rabuka officiated at the groundbreaking ceremony on Thursday, describing the investment as a sign of confidence in Fiji’s economic future and its potential to compete in international timber markets.

“Today marks a significant milestone, not only for Tropik Wood Industries and Fiji Pine Group, but for the future of the forestry sector and our broader economic transformation journey,” Mr Rabuka said.

The new sawmill will allow Tropik Wood Industries to diversify into hardwood processing, an area it has not previously undertaken, while creating opportunities in manufacturing, skills development and employment.

“With an investment of approximately $35million, this project reflects confidence in the future of Fiji’s forestry and our ability to compete in international markets.”

Mr Rabuka said the project aligned with the Government’s vision to build a resilient and prosperous economy by ensuring natural resources were sustainably managed and used to create long-term benefits.

“By strengthening our timber processing capacity, Fiji will retain greater economic value within the country, create more opportunities for local businesses, and generate stronger returns from our forest resources,” he said.

Fiji Pine Group chief executive officer Ratu Rakuita Vakalalabure said the sawmill would improve efficiency, promote value addition, support employment and strengthen sustainability in the forestry industry.

item.content:encoded:
JUSTICE Dane Tuiqereqere has raised concerns about the transparency of the Barbara Malimali Commission of Inquiry (COI), questioning the use of closed sessions and the lack of documented reasons for excluding individuals from hearings.

At a court mention yesterday, Justice Tuiqereqere questioned the COI’s use of unexplained “closed sessions” and requested clarification regarding why Ms Malimali and her lawyer were excluded from key hearings.

Justice Tuiqereqere is hearing three separate legal challenges to the findings of the COI into the appointment of Ms Malimali as Commissioner of the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption.

Ms Malimali, together with senior lawyers Wylie Clarke and Laurel Vaurasi and former Attorney-General Graham Leung have all sought judicial review of the COI’s findings against them.

Justice Tuiqereqere called the lawyers for the parties together yesterday for answers to specific questions he wished to raise before issuing his judgment, which he said would now take place on August 10.

He said he had reviewed the COI report and transcripts of the evidence given but did not know what reason the COI had given for excluding Ms Malimali and her lawyers from some of the hearings.

He expressed concern about the state of the COI record, noting that proceedings of such public importance should be accurate. He said natural justice demanded clear, documented reasons when individuals were excluded.

Deputy Solicitor-General Eliesa Tuiloma said he was unaware of any official justification provided by COI Commissioner Justice David Ashton-Lewis for excluding Ms Malimali during testimony from key witnesses, including the Chief Justice and former Finance Minister Professor Biman Prasad.

The court’s ruling on the judicial review has been moved from August 3 to August 10.

item.title: Motive behind fatal fire questioned
item.description: THE High Court has queried the alleged motive of Reana Devi Chand, a woman charged with murder, observing that it would appear illogical for her to destroy a property she was allegedly expecting to own. Ms Chand made her first appearance before Justice Daniel Goundar in Suva yesterday, charged with one count of murder allegedly committed on December 24 last year.
item.content:encoded:
THE High Court has queried the alleged motive of Reana Devi Chand, a woman charged with murder, observing that it would appear illogical for her to destroy a property she was allegedly expecting to own.

Ms Chand made her first appearance before Justice Daniel Goundar in Suva yesterday, charged with one count of murder allegedly committed on December 24 last year.

Prosecutor Hezekiah Nofaga told the court the alleged motive stemmed from a dispute between Ms Chand and the landlady over the property.

The State alleges Ms Chand caused the death of a 19-year-old woman after intentionally setting fire to a flat on Levuka St, Samabula. It is alleged that Ms Chand started the fire after a prior arrangement to purchase the property failed to eventuate, resulting in the victim becoming trapped inside the house and dying.

The court was also told there was no information confirming any history of mental illness or violence involving Ms Chand. Defence lawyer Patrick Kumar said he was not seeking a psychiatric evaluation of his client at this stage.

The court heard Ms Chand is employed as a dental clerk at the Colonial War Memorial Hospital under the Ministry of Health.

Ms Chand was further remanded, with the matter adjourned to September 4 for plea.

item.content:encoded:
FIJI’S import bill for petroleum products such as petrol, diesel and jet fuel has risen sharply in recent months, with imports of mineral fuels for the first four months of this year totalling $656.2 million, 36.3 per cent higher than the same period in 2025.

ANZ senior Pacific economist Dr Kishti Sen and senior Commodity Strategist Daniel Hynes said this was driven by higher crude oil prices and a rise in refining margins.

“We expect them to remain elevated even if the Middle East conflict ends,” the duo said in the bank’s Pacific Insight report obtained by The Fiji Times.

“The ongoing control of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran will keep oil flows constrained and should see crude oil prices stay near the $US90/bbl level through to the end of the year.

“Hence, we think Fiji’s mineral fuel imports are likely to hit an all-time high of $2,000m in 2026, pushing the current account deficit to $1,500m from $1,039m in 2025.”

Dr Sen and Mr Hynes said this deficit would be paid for by capital inflows and via a drawdown on the nation’s foreign reserves. “Despite the drawdown, we still see Fiji carrying sufficient buffer of foreign reserves.

“We don’t envisage any significant changes to exchange control rules and regulations on capital outflows.”

The report stated that the risk of ongoing attacks on vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz under Iranian control would likely see a geopolitical risk premium embedded in prices.

“Moreover, heavily depleted inventories have significantly reduced the oil market’s buffer against future supply disruptions.

“This should keep Brent crude above $US90/bbl for the remainder of 2026.

“Combined with elevated shipping costs, this will likely push up Fiji’s fuel imports to $FJ2,000m in 2026, 25.9 per cent higher than in 2025 and the current account deficit to $FJ1,500m.”

item.title: Bank launches lending centre
item.description: People around Lami and nearby areas will now have better loan services provided after the launch of the ANZ lending branch at the Harbour Point in Lami on Thursday. The new lending centre will provide assistance to customers with personalised and face-to-face lending services while understanding peoples neeeds and requirements in an increasingly digital banking environment.
item.content:encoded:
People around Lami and nearby areas will now have better loan services provided after the launch of the ANZ lending branch at the Harbour Point in Lami on Thursday.

The new lending centre will provide assistance to customers with personalised and face-to-face lending services while understanding peoples neeeds and requirements in an increasingly digital banking environment.

ANZ country head Fiji Sohaib Mahmood said the new centre reflected the bank’s long-standing commitment to serving communities through human interaction, despite the rapid growth of digital banking and artificial intelligence.

“The centre has been established to provide customers with tailored lending solutions through one-on-one consultations, recognising that not all financial situations can be addressed through digital applications alone, ” Mr Mahmood said at the launch.

“Not all lending is simple, and not every customer’s situation fits into a standard form,” he said.

He said this centre would allow the opportunity for officers to sit down with customers, understand their needs and develop solutions that work for them.

ANZ Pacific regional executive Sarah Stubbings said the new lending initiative was aimed at helping customers achieve important financial goals, including purchasing homes, financing personal needs, and buying vehicles.

“We’re supporting our customers who want to buy a house, take out a personal loan to support their families, or finance a vehicle,” Ms Stubbings said.

“It’s a different model for us, and we haven’t done something like this in Fiji before,” she said.

The lending centre will operate during normal business hours and welcomes both appointments and walk-in customers seeking lending advice.

ANZ Regional Executive Pacific Sarah Stubbings (third from left) and Sohaib Mahmood, ANZ Fiji Country Head and Head of Commercial Pacific (sixth from left) are joined by ANZ Retail team members to celebrate the new Lami Lending Centre. Picture: SUPPLIED

item.title: Families need more support, not blame, says report
item.description: THE responsibility of caring for children living with disabilities in Fiji should be shared by the wider community, not placed solely on parents. This was the message from Fiji Human Rights Commissioner Veena Singh as she responded to concerns about a growing number of parental neglect cases involving children living with disabilities.
item.content:encoded:
THE responsibility of caring for children living with disabilities in Fiji should be shared by the wider community, not placed solely on parents.

This was the message from Fiji Human Rights Commissioner Veena Singh as she responded to concerns about a growing number of parental neglect cases involving children living with disabilities.

Ms Singh said understanding the different types of disabilities was the first step towards creating a more supportive and inclusive society.

She said caring for children with disabilities was a shared responsibility and that communities, the media and institutions all had a role to play in supporting families.

“The parents can do what they can with what is available to them, but also as a community,” Ms Singh said.

“The media could help by increasing communication, visibility and awareness, while the Human Rights Commission would continue amplifying the issue to reduce the burden on individual families.”

Ms Singh said reports of neglect should be viewed within a broader context rather than placing blame on parents alone.

Lead report writer for the Baseline Study on Rights of Children with Disabilities in Fiji, Kayt Bronnimann said parents also needed to be empowered with the information and support required to raise a child with a disability.

She said the study found this was not always the case.

“The focus should be on creating a supportive environment rather than pointing fingers at parents,” Ms Bronnimann said.

She said government and organisations had a responsibility to ensure families had access to the information, disability allowances and respite care needed to support children living with disabilities.

“So (providing) these, instances of neglect hopefully will just be isolated cases and that we really want to focus on empowering and supporting parents to be able to care for their children.”

item.title: Grandfather calls for better disability services
item.description: A NATIONS prosperity will be determined by how it cares for its most vulnerable. This was shared by Meli Namasala, grandfather of 13-year-old Jaeli Rosituyawa Radniceva, a child living with albinism and a visual impairment, whose grandfathers unwavering support has become the foundation of her life.
item.content:encoded:
A NATIONS prosperity will be determined by how it cares for its most vulnerable.

This was shared by Meli Namasala, grandfather of 13-year-old Jaeli Rosituyawa Radniceva, a child living with albinism and a visual impairment, whose grandfathers unwavering support has become the foundation of her life.

Speaking to the media yesterday, Mr Namasala said he knew from the moment he first saw his granddaughter that she would need extra love and care.

Mr Namasala said he returned home from Syria in 2014 determined to help provide for Jaeli and support her parents.

He said he later encouraged Jaeli’s grandmother to take over her care after they noticed her mother was struggling to accept her.

“It should be our responsibility now to step in and support and take good care of her,” he recalled saying.

“Jaeli later moved with her mother to Suva to attend school in Vatuwaqa but often called, asking to return to back home to us.”

He said she told them she was not receiving enough food and that some of her needs were being neglected.

The family eventually brought Jaeli back home and enrolled her at Dilkusha School.

Mr Namasala said she is now in Year 7 after facing academic setbacks linked to the challenges she had experienced.

Reflecting on his family’s journey, he urged parents to embrace children with disabilities rather than reject them.

“My advice to the parents with kids that require special needs and care is that, ‘It’s a blessing to have one of this kind at home’.”

Mr Namasala said caring for children with disabilities was not only a family responsibility but one that reflected the values of a nation.

“The prosperity of any nation depends on how we look after the disabled, the underprivileged… like my granddaughter here.”

He also called on the Government to continue improving services for children with disabilities and thanked the programme for giving families an opportunity to share their experiences.

item.title: Rabuka denies road privilege
item.description: PRIME Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says his village still relies on a gravel road nearly 70 years after it was built, rejecting claims that his constituency has received preferential Government treatment. Mr Rabuka said little had changed since the road was constructed in 1956.
item.content:encoded:
PRIME Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says his village still relies on a gravel road nearly 70 years after it was built, rejecting claims that his constituency has received preferential Government treatment.

Mr Rabuka said little had changed since the road was constructed in 1956.

“If you were driving down from the village this morning, you would have travelled along the Cakaudrove road,” he said.

“That road was built back in 1956. It was a gravel road then, and it is still a gravel road today.”

He said the branch road leading to his village was completed in 1974 while he was serving with the British Guards in Hong Kong, but it also remained unsealed.

However, Mr Rabuka said many communities across Fiji continued to raise concerns about poor road infrastructure.

“Many parts of Fiji are complaining that their roads are still not sealed.”

Mr Rabuka said his province and area had not received special treatment, despite recent claims in the media.

“They should go back and tell them that it is certainly not the Prime Minister’s area that has received special treatment.”

He said the condition of roads in his area showed that many rural communities were still waiting for improved infrastructure.
